# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is lazy. Left to itself, it sits still, and when it does move, it only moves downhill. Everything about a municipal water system is an elaborate argument with this basic fact of physics. To understand how a city delivers water to a thirty-story apartment building, you have to follow the energy budget of every drop, from the reservoir to the showerhead on the top floor.

## The Fundamental Currency: Hydraulic Head

Engineers talk about water pressure in terms of "head," which is simply the height of a column of water. Every 10 meters (about 33 feet) of elevation corresponds to roughly one atmosphere of pressure, or about 14.7 pounds per square inch. If you hold a vertical pipe full of water, the pressure at the bottom depends only on how tall the column is—gravity does all the work.

This is why cities are so often built around reservoirs placed high up. New York City, for instance, gets much of its water from reservoirs in the Catskill Mountains, more than a hundred miles away, and the water arrives with enough residual pressure to serve buildings several stories tall without any pumping at all.
